Janet: Could you come and help me with the printer please?
Secretary: Certainly. What seems to be the problem with it? Is there a paper jam?
Janet: No. Yesterday all my documents were coming out streaky and I was having trouble with duplex printing as well. Today the printer is not printing at all!
Secretary: Has it gotten unplugged?
Janet: No, the lights are on and it's running.

Secretary: You said it was printing poorly yesterday but at least it was producing. Would you mind checking if to see it has run out of paper? Check each of the input trays.
Janet: Let's see. No, that doesn't seem to be the problem. There is plenty of paper in all of those and the multipurpose trays.
Secretary: Does the dialogue box correspond with what you selected? Check the printer's pop-up menu.
Janet: Surprisingly there is no alert message on the printer display.

Secretary: Did you say that your documents came out spotty yesterday?
Janet: Yes. However nothing is happening today. You can hear the machine running but there is no output or indication of what the problem may be. Should we call in a technician?
Secretary: I think it is our only option. Should I contact a printer repair company or call in Joe?
Janet: I'd call Joe. We know that he is competent and what he charges. A large company will cost more and their service may not be any better.

Using the Continuous Tenses to Describe Technical Problems

The Continuous Tenses are used to express the idea that something is or was happening at the moment of speaking. It can be used to describe technical problems you might encounter with technology in the workplace.
Look at the charts below to read about how the tenses are formed:

You can use the Past or Present Continuous tense to describe actions that are or were happening at the moment of speaking.

• My internet is not working at all!
  • My computer was producing yesterday.
The Past and Present Continuous are also used to describe actions or situations that were in progress around the present or past time, but not necessarily at the moment of speaking.

• Rick: Hey, what were you doing in the cafeteria this morning?
    Bill: I was taking a break but I'm fixing Marie's printer.
Contractions are often used in spoken English. When using the Present Continuous tense people more frequently use “‘s not/‘re not + -ing” than “isn't/aren't + -ing”.
• The lights aren't running on the printer.
Asking For and Offering Help with Technical Problems

Often in the workplace, you will have issues with technology. Your printer may stop printing, your internet may stop working, and your screen may freeze. When you face any of these issues, you will need to ask for help and sometimes offer help with these problems. Here's some language you can use:

• Use modal verbs to ask for help with technical problems.
    • Could you help me connect to the internet, please?
    • Should we call in someone?
    • Would you mind checking if it has run out of ink?

• Use imperatives (the base form of the verb) to tell people to do something.
    • Check the paper trays.
    • Make sure it is working.

• UUse the Present Simple tense to ask questions or when troubleshooting.
    • What seems to be the problem?
    • There is a signal coming from the modem.
    • Does it correspond with what you see on your computer?
